CHAPTER 10 - LINES AND ANGLES

Introduction

Geometry begins with a few simple ideas - the point, the line and the angle - out of which the whole subject is built. In this chapter we revisit these basic terms, learn how angles are measured, classify angles by size, and study how angles behave when they occur in pairs. The most important results concern a pair of PARALLEL LINES cut by a TRANSVERSAL: these give a set of equal and supplementary angles that are used again and again in later chapters (triangles, quadrilaterals, circles). We finish with 'angle-chasing' - the technique of finding an unknown angle by applying these rules step by step.

10.1 BASIC TERMS: POINT, LINE, RAY, LINE SEGMENT

A POINT is a location. It has no length, breadth or thickness - only position. A point is drawn as a tiny dot and named with a capital letter, for example the point P.

A LINE is a straight arrangement of points that extends without end in BOTH directions. We show this with arrowheads at both ends. A line through two points A and B is written as line AB, and it has no fixed length.

A LINE SEGMENT is the part of a line between two endpoints. The segment from A to B is written AB and it has a definite length - the distance between A and B. Unlike a line, it does not extend beyond its endpoints.

A RAY starts at one endpoint and extends without end in ONE direction. The ray starting at A and passing through B is written ray AB; A is the endpoint. A ray has one endpoint and no fixed length.

Two other useful ideas:
- COLLINEAR POINTS are points that lie on one straight line.
- CONCURRENT LINES are three or more lines that pass through a single common point.

10.2 ANGLE AND ITS MEASURE

An ANGLE is formed when two rays start from the same endpoint. The common endpoint is the VERTEX, and the two rays are the ARMS (or sides) of the angle. If the two arms are ray BA and ray BC, the angle is named angle ABC (or angle CBA), with the vertex letter B always in the MIDDLE. When there is no confusion it may simply be called angle B.

The SIZE of an angle measures the amount of turning between the two arms, NOT the length of the arms. Angles are measured in DEGREES using a protractor. One full turn is divided into 360 equal parts; each part is one degree, written 1°. Thus a complete revolution is 360°, a half turn is 180°, and a quarter turn is 90°.

10.3 TYPES OF ANGLES

Angles are classified by their measure:
- ACUTE ANGLE: greater than 0° and less than 90°. Example: 45°, 60°.
- RIGHT ANGLE: exactly 90°. Its arms are perpendicular. A small square at the vertex marks a right angle.
- OBTUSE ANGLE: greater than 90° but less than 180°. Example: 120°, 135°.
- STRAIGHT ANGLE: exactly 180°. The two arms point in opposite directions and form a straight line.
- REFLEX ANGLE: greater than 180° but less than 360°. Example: 210°, 300°.
- COMPLETE ANGLE (full angle): exactly 360° - one full revolution.

A ZERO ANGLE is 0°, when the two arms coincide. Note that the reflex angle and the ordinary ('interior') angle at the same vertex together make 360°. For an ordinary angle of 100°, the reflex angle on the other side is 360° - 100° = 260°.

10.4 COMPLEMENTARY AND SUPPLEMENTARY ANGLES

Two angles are COMPLEMENTARY if their measures add up to 90°. Each is called the COMPLEMENT of the other. For example, 30° and 60° are complementary because 30° + 60° = 90°. The complement of an angle x is (90° - x). Only an acute angle has a complement.

Two angles are SUPPLEMENTARY if their measures add up to 180°. Each is the SUPPLEMENT of the other. For example, 110° and 70° are supplementary because 110° + 70° = 180°. The supplement of an angle x is (180° - x). An acute or an obtuse angle (or a right angle) can have a supplement.

Worked example: If an angle is 35°, its complement is 90° - 35° = 55° and its supplement is 180° - 35° = 145°.

Worked example: Find an angle that is equal to its own complement. Let the angle be x. Then x + x = 90°, so 2x = 90° and x = 45°. Similarly the angle equal to its own supplement is 90°.

10.5 ADJACENT ANGLES AND LINEAR PAIR

Two angles are ADJACENT if they have (i) the same vertex, (ii) a common arm, and (iii) their other (non-common) arms lie on opposite sides of the common arm. In other words the two angles sit side by side without overlapping. For example, if ray OB stands between ray OA and ray OC, then angle AOB and angle BOC are adjacent, sharing the common arm OB.

A LINEAR PAIR is a pair of adjacent angles whose non-common arms form a straight line (point in opposite directions). Because the outer arms make a straight angle, the two angles of a linear pair ADD UP TO 180° - they are supplementary. This is the LINEAR PAIR AXIOM: if a ray stands on a straight line, the two adjacent angles so formed are supplementary. Conversely, if two adjacent angles are supplementary, their outer arms form a straight line.

Worked example: A ray stands on a line making two adjacent angles. If one is 65°, the other is 180° - 65° = 115°.

Angles about a point: if several rays start from one point, all the angles formed around that point add up to 360° (angles at a point).

10.6 VERTICALLY OPPOSITE ANGLES

When two straight lines cross (intersect), four angles are formed at the point of intersection. The angles that are OPPOSITE each other (not adjacent) are called VERTICALLY OPPOSITE ANGLES. There are two such pairs.

THEOREM: Vertically opposite angles are equal.

Proof: Let lines AB and CD cross at O, forming angle AOC, angle COB, angle BOD and angle DOA (going around). AOC and COB form a linear pair on line AB, so angle AOC + angle COB = 180°. Also COB and BOD form a linear pair on line CD, so angle COB + angle BOD = 180°. Therefore angle AOC + angle COB = angle COB + angle BOD. Cancelling angle COB from both sides gives angle AOC = angle BOD. Similarly angle COB = angle DOA. Hence vertically opposite angles are equal.

Worked example: Two lines cross and one of the four angles is 50°. Then its vertically opposite angle is also 50°, and each of the other two angles is 180° - 50° = 130° (they form linear pairs with the 50° angle).

10.7 PARALLEL LINES AND A TRANSVERSAL

Two lines in a plane are PARALLEL if they never meet, no matter how far they are extended. We write AB || CD to mean line AB is parallel to line CD. The perpendicular distance between two parallel lines is always the same.

A TRANSVERSAL is a line that cuts two (or more) other lines at distinct points. When a transversal crosses two lines it makes EIGHT angles - four at each crossing. These angles are given special names by their position:

- CORRESPONDING ANGLES: a pair in the same position at the two crossings (for example, both above the cut line and both on the left). There are four such pairs.
- ALTERNATE INTERIOR ANGLES: a pair between the two lines (interior) but on opposite sides of the transversal. There are two such pairs.
- ALTERNATE EXTERIOR ANGLES: a pair outside the two lines (exterior) and on opposite sides of the transversal. Two such pairs.
- CO-INTERIOR ANGLES (also called ALLIED or CONSECUTIVE INTERIOR angles): a pair between the two lines and on the SAME side of the transversal. Two such pairs.

When the two lines are PARALLEL, these angle pairs satisfy:
- Corresponding angles are EQUAL.
- Alternate interior angles are EQUAL.
- Alternate exterior angles are EQUAL.
- Co-interior (allied) angles are SUPPLEMENTARY (add up to 180°).

These follow from one basic assumption (the corresponding-angles axiom): if a transversal cuts two parallel lines, each pair of corresponding angles is equal. From it, the alternate-angle and co-interior results are proved using vertically opposite angles and linear pairs.

Worked example: Lines l and m are parallel, cut by a transversal. One angle is 70°. Then its corresponding angle is 70°; the alternate interior angle equal to it is 70°; and the co-interior angle on the same side is 180° - 70° = 110°.

10.8 CONDITIONS FOR TWO LINES TO BE PARALLEL

The results above can be reversed to TEST whether two lines are parallel. If a transversal cuts two lines such that ANY ONE of the following holds, then the two lines are parallel:
- a pair of corresponding angles are equal, OR
- a pair of alternate interior angles are equal, OR
- a pair of alternate exterior angles are equal, OR
- a pair of co-interior (allied) angles are supplementary (sum 180°).

Also, two lines that are each parallel to the same line are parallel to each other. And two lines perpendicular to the same line are parallel.

10.9 ANGLE-CHASING: WORKED PROBLEMS

Angle-chasing means finding unknown angles step by step, quoting a reason at each step (linear pair, vertically opposite, corresponding, alternate, co-interior).

Example 1: In the figure AB || CD, and a transversal makes an angle of 120° with AB at the upper crossing (measured on one side). Find the co-interior angle at CD. Since co-interior angles are supplementary, the required angle = 180° - 120° = 60°.

Example 2: Two lines meet a transversal so that a pair of alternate interior angles are 3x and (x + 40)°. If the lines are parallel, alternate interior angles are equal: 3x = x + 40, so 2x = 40 and x = 20. The angles are 60° each.

Example 3: A ray OP stands on line MN at O. Angle MOP = (2x + 10)° and angle PON = (3x - 30)° form a linear pair, so their sum is 180°: (2x + 10) + (3x - 30) = 180, giving 5x - 20 = 180, 5x = 200, x = 40. Then angle MOP = 90° and angle PON = 90°.

Example 4 (parallel test): A transversal cuts two lines making co-interior angles 105° and 75°. Their sum is 180°, so the two lines ARE parallel.

SUMMARY

- A point marks position; a line extends endlessly both ways; a segment has two endpoints and a definite length; a ray has one endpoint and extends one way.
- An angle is formed by two rays from a common vertex; its size (in degrees) measures turning, not arm length. One full turn = 360°.
- Angle types: acute (<90°), right (=90°), obtuse (90°-180°), straight (=180°), reflex (180°-360°), complete (=360°).
- Complementary angles sum to 90°; supplementary angles sum to 180°.
- Adjacent angles share a vertex and an arm. A linear pair is adjacent and supplementary (outer arms make a straight line). Angles around a point sum to 360°.
- Vertically opposite angles (formed by two crossing lines) are equal.
- For two PARALLEL lines cut by a transversal: corresponding angles equal; alternate interior angles equal; alternate exterior angles equal; co-interior (allied) angles supplementary.
- These converse conditions test parallelism. Lines parallel to the same line are parallel; lines perpendicular to the same line are parallel.
- Angle-chasing solves for unknown angles by applying these rules in sequence, giving a reason at each step.

chapter_summary.title: Lines and Angles - Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This chapter builds geometry from its basic terms - point, line, ray and segment - then studies angles: how they are measured, how they are classified, and how they pair up. The key results are the equality of vertically opposite angles and the angle relations for parallel lines cut by a transversal, used everywhere in later geometry.

sections.heading: Basic terms
bullets: A point marks a position and has no length, breadth or thickness.
A line extends endlessly in both directions; a line segment is the part between two endpoints and has a definite length; a ray has one endpoint and extends endlessly in one direction.
Collinear points lie on one line; concurrent lines pass through one common point.

sections.heading: Angles and their types
bullets: An angle is formed by two rays (arms) meeting at a common endpoint (the vertex); it is named with the vertex letter in the middle, e.g. angle ABC.
Angle size measures turning, in degrees; a full turn is 360 degrees, a half turn 180 degrees, a quarter turn 90 degrees.
Types: acute (<90), right (=90), obtuse (90-180), straight (=180), reflex (180-360), complete (=360).

sections.heading: Complementary, supplementary and adjacent angles
bullets: Complementary angles add up to 90 degrees; the complement of x is (90 - x). Only acute angles have complements.
Supplementary angles add up to 180 degrees; the supplement of x is (180 - x).
Adjacent angles share a vertex and a common arm with their other arms on opposite sides; a linear pair is adjacent and supplementary.
Angles around a point add up to 360 degrees.

sections.heading: Vertically opposite angles
bullets: When two lines cross, four angles are formed; the opposite (non-adjacent) pairs are vertically opposite angles.
Vertically opposite angles are equal - proved using two linear pairs.
If one of the four angles is known, the opposite one equals it and each adjacent one is its supplement.

sections.heading: Parallel lines cut by a transversal
bullets: A transversal cutting two lines makes eight angles: corresponding, alternate interior, alternate exterior and co-interior (allied) pairs.
For parallel lines: corresponding angles are equal, alternate interior and alternate exterior angles are equal, and co-interior angles are supplementary.
Conversely, if any such condition holds for a transversal, the two lines are parallel; lines parallel (or perpendicular) to the same line are parallel to each other.

key_takeaways: Point, line, segment and ray are the basic undefined/derived terms; only the segment has a fixed length.
An angle's size is measured in degrees; a full turn is 360 degrees. Angles are acute, right, obtuse, straight, reflex or complete.
Complementary angles sum to 90 degrees; supplementary angles sum to 180 degrees.
A linear pair is supplementary; angles at a point sum to 360 degrees.
For parallel lines cut by a transversal: corresponding and alternate angles are equal; co-interior (allied) angles are supplementary.
The converse angle conditions test whether two lines are parallel; angle-chasing applies all these rules step by step.

glossary.definition: A location with no length, breadth or thickness; shown as a dot and named by a capital letter.
A straight set of points extending endlessly in both directions; has no fixed length.
The part of a line between two endpoints; it has a definite length equal to the distance between the endpoints.
A part of a line with one endpoint that extends endlessly in one direction.
The figure formed by two rays (arms) with a common endpoint called the vertex; measured in degrees.
An angle greater than 0 degrees and less than 90 degrees.
An angle of exactly 90 degrees; its arms are perpendicular.
An angle greater than 90 degrees and less than 180 degrees.
An angle greater than 180 degrees and less than 360 degrees.
Two angles whose measures add up to 90 degrees; each is the complement of the other.
Two angles whose measures add up to 180 degrees; each is the supplement of the other.
A pair of adjacent angles whose non-common arms form a straight line; they are supplementary (sum 180 degrees).
The opposite (non-adjacent) angles formed when two lines cross; they are equal.
A line that cuts two or more other lines at distinct points, forming eight angles with a pair of lines.
Interior angles on the same side of a transversal (allied angles); supplementary when the lines are parallel.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Lines and Angles
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Draw rough figures where helpful and give a reason for each step in angle-chasing problems. Marks are shown against each question.

questions.question: Define, with correct notation: (a) a line segment, (b) a ray. State one way each differs from a full line.
questions.answer:
(a) A LINE SEGMENT is the part of a line between two endpoints A and B, written AB. It has a DEFINITE length (the distance AB) and does NOT extend beyond its endpoints. A full line, by contrast, has no endpoints and no fixed length.
(b) A RAY starts at one endpoint A and extends endlessly in one direction through B, written ray AB. It has ONE endpoint and no fixed length. A full line has NO endpoints and extends both ways.
So: segment = two endpoints (finite); ray = one endpoint (half-infinite); line = no endpoints (infinite both ways).
questions.explanation: Compare endpoints and length with a full line.

questions.question: Classify each angle: 42°, 90°, 118°, 180°, 245°, 360°.
questions.answer:
42° - ACUTE (between 0° and 90°).
90° - RIGHT angle.
118° - OBTUSE (between 90° and 180°).
180° - STRAIGHT angle.
245° - REFLEX (between 180° and 360°).
360° - COMPLETE (full) angle.
questions.explanation: Use the standard measure ranges for each angle type.

questions.question: Find the complement and the supplement of 37°.
questions.answer:
Complement = 90° - 37° = 53°.
Supplement = 180° - 37° = 143°.
Check: 37° + 53° = 90° and 37° + 143° = 180°. Both correct.

questions.question: Two supplementary angles are in the ratio 2 : 3. Find both angles.
questions.answer:
Let the angles be 2x and 3x. Being supplementary, 2x + 3x = 180°.
So 5x = 180°, giving x = 36°.
The angles are 2x = 72° and 3x = 108°.
Check: 72° + 108° = 180°. Correct.
questions.explanation: Set up ratio parts, use the sum 180, solve for x.

questions.question: A ray OC stands on a line AOB. If angle AOC = (3x + 5)° and angle COB = (2x - 25)° form a linear pair, find x and both angles.
questions.answer:
A ray on a line makes a LINEAR PAIR, which is supplementary:
(3x + 5) + (2x - 25) = 180.
5x - 20 = 180, so 5x = 200 and x = 40.
angle AOC = 3(40) + 5 = 125°.
angle COB = 2(40) - 25 = 55°.
Check: 125° + 55° = 180°. Correct.
questions.explanation: Linear pair sum = 180; solve the linear equation.

questions.question: Two straight lines AB and CD intersect at O. If angle AOC = 65°, find the other three angles, giving reasons.
questions.answer:
angle BOD = angle AOC = 65° (vertically opposite angles).
angle AOC and angle AOD form a linear pair on line CD, so angle AOD = 180° - 65° = 115°.
angle BOC = angle AOD = 115° (vertically opposite angles).
So the four angles are 65°, 115°, 65°, 115°.
questions.explanation: Vertically opposite equal; adjacent form linear pairs.

questions.question: Prove that vertically opposite angles are equal. Use two intersecting lines AB and CD meeting at O.
questions.answer:
Given: lines AB and CD intersect at O, forming angles AOC, COB, BOD and DOA around O.
To prove: angle AOC = angle BOD (and angle COB = angle AOD).
Proof: Ray OC stands on line AB, so angle AOC and angle COB form a linear pair:
  angle AOC + angle COB = 180°   ... (1)
Ray OB stands on line CD, so angle COB and angle BOD form a linear pair:
  angle COB + angle BOD = 180°   ... (2)
From (1) and (2): angle AOC + angle COB = angle COB + angle BOD.
Subtract angle COB from both sides: angle AOC = angle BOD.
Similarly, angle COB = angle AOD. Hence vertically opposite angles are equal. QED.
questions.explanation: Two linear pairs share the common angle COB; cancel it.

questions.question: In the figure AB || CD and a transversal cuts them. One interior angle at AB is 108°. Find (a) its co-interior angle at CD, (b) the alternate interior angle at CD.
questions.answer:
(a) Co-interior (allied) angles are supplementary for parallel lines:
  required = 180° - 108° = 72°.
(b) Alternate interior angles are equal for parallel lines:
  required = 108°.
So the co-interior angle is 72° and the alternate interior angle is 108°.

questions.question: A transversal cuts two lines so that a pair of co-interior angles measure 97° and 83°. Are the two lines parallel? Justify.
questions.answer:
Add the co-interior angles: 97° + 83° = 180°.
By the converse condition, if co-interior (allied) angles are SUPPLEMENTARY, the two lines are PARALLEL.
Since the sum is exactly 180°, the two lines ARE parallel.

questions.question: In the figure, AB || CD. A transversal makes an angle of 3x with AB, and the co-interior angle at CD is 2x. Find x and both angles. Then state the corresponding angle to the 3x angle.
questions.answer:
Co-interior angles between parallel lines are supplementary:
  3x + 2x = 180°.
  5x = 180°, so x = 36°.
The angle at AB = 3x = 108°; the co-interior angle at CD = 2x = 72°.
Check: 108° + 72° = 180°. Correct.
The corresponding angle to the 108° angle is also 108° (corresponding angles between parallel lines are equal).
questions.explanation: Co-interior supplementary gives x; corresponding angles equal.

An angle greater than 180° and less than 360° is a ____ angle.
The complement of 25° is ____.
The supplement of 95° is ____.
An angle equal to its own supplement measures ____.
The angles of a ____ pair add up to 180°.
All the angles around a point add up to ____.
Two lines intersect; one angle is 55°, so its vertically opposite angle is ____.
A line cutting two other lines at distinct points is called a ____.
For parallel lines, ____ angles are supplementary.
AB || CD; a co-interior angle to 115° measures ____.
AB || CD; the corresponding angle to 72° measures ____.
Distinguish between a line and a line segment.
questions.answer: A LINE extends endlessly in both directions and has NO fixed length (drawn with arrowheads at both ends). A LINE SEGMENT is the part of a line between two endpoints; it has a DEFINITE length and does not extend beyond its endpoints. So a segment is a bounded piece of a line.

questions.question: What are collinear points and concurrent lines?
questions.answer: COLLINEAR POINTS are points that all lie on one single straight line. CONCURRENT LINES are three or more lines that all pass through one common point. So 'collinear' is a property of points; 'concurrent' is a property of lines.
questions.explanation: Collinear = points on a line; concurrent = lines through a point.

questions.question: Explain why ray AB and ray BA are not the same.
questions.answer: A ray is named by its endpoint first. Ray AB has endpoint A and goes through B, extending beyond B. Ray BA has endpoint B and goes through A, extending beyond A. They start at different points and point in opposite directions, so they are different rays even though both lie on line AB.

questions.question: Name the parts of an angle and how an angle is named.
questions.answer: An angle has a VERTEX (the common endpoint of the two rays) and two ARMS or sides (the rays). It is named by three letters with the vertex letter in the MIDDLE, e.g. angle ABC has vertex B and arms BA and BC. When unambiguous it may be called angle B.
questions.explanation: Vertex + two arms; vertex letter in the middle.

questions.question: Classify: 15°, 90°, 100°, 180°, 300°.
questions.answer: 15° - acute (0-90). 90° - right angle. 100° - obtuse (90-180). 180° - straight angle. 300° - reflex (180-360).
questions.explanation: Match each measure to its range.

questions.question: Why does the length of the arms not change the size of an angle?
questions.answer: The size of an angle measures the AMOUNT OF TURNING (opening) between the two arms, not how long the arms are drawn. If you extend both arms, the opening between them stays the same, so the angle is unchanged. That is why a protractor reading does not depend on arm length.
questions.explanation: Angle = turning, independent of arm length.

questions.question: An angle measures 145°. Find the reflex angle at the same vertex.
questions.answer:
The ordinary angle and its reflex together make a full turn of 360°.
Reflex angle = 360° - 145° = 215°.

questions.question: Find the complement and supplement of 62°.
Two complementary angles are in the ratio 4 : 5. Find them.
questions.answer:
Let the angles be 4x and 5x. Complementary means 4x + 5x = 90°.
9x = 90°, so x = 10°.
The angles are 40° and 50°. Check: 40 + 50 = 90. Correct.
questions.explanation: Sum of parts = 90; solve for x.

questions.question: The supplement of an angle is 4 times the angle. Find the angle.
questions.answer:
Let the angle be x. Its supplement is 180° - x, and this equals 4x.
180° - x = 4x => 180° = 5x => x = 36°.
The angle is 36° and its supplement is 144°.

questions.question: An angle is 30° less than twice its supplement. Find the angle.
questions.answer:
Let the angle be x, so its supplement is 180° - x.
Given x = 2(180° - x) - 30°.
x = 360° - 2x - 30° => x + 2x = 330° => 3x = 330° => x = 110°.
So the angle is 110° (its supplement is 70°).

questions.question: State the conditions for two angles to be adjacent.
questions.answer: Two angles are adjacent if: (i) they have the SAME vertex, (ii) they have a COMMON arm, and (iii) their other (non-common) arms lie on OPPOSITE sides of the common arm (so the angles do not overlap).
questions.explanation: Common vertex, common arm, non-common arms on opposite sides.

questions.question: What is a linear pair? State the linear-pair axiom.
questions.answer: A LINEAR PAIR is a pair of adjacent angles whose non-common arms form a straight line (opposite rays). LINEAR-PAIR AXIOM: if a ray stands on a straight line, the two adjacent angles so formed are supplementary (their sum is 180°). Conversely, if two adjacent angles are supplementary, their outer arms form a straight line.
questions.explanation: Adjacent + outer arms opposite rays => supplementary.

questions.question: Explain why angles around a point add up to 360°.
questions.answer: The rays drawn from a single point divide the full turn around that point into several angles. Since one complete revolution about a point is 360°, all the angles formed around the point together fill that revolution and so add up to 360°.

questions.question: A ray stands on a line making angles 3x and 2x. Find x and both angles.
questions.answer:
The two angles form a linear pair, so 3x + 2x = 180°.
5x = 180° => x = 36°.
The angles are 3x = 108° and 2x = 72°. Check: 108 + 72 = 180.

questions.question: Two lines intersect at O. angle AOC = (2x + 15)° and its vertically opposite angle BOD = (3x - 25)°. Find x and the angle.
questions.answer:
Vertically opposite angles are equal: 2x + 15 = 3x - 25.
15 + 25 = 3x - 2x => x = 40.
angle AOC = 2(40) + 15 = 95° (and angle BOD = 95°).
questions.explanation: Set the two equal, solve for x.

questions.question: Two lines cross; one of the four angles is 118°. Find the other three, with reasons.
questions.answer:
The vertically opposite angle = 118° (vertically opposite angles equal).
Each adjacent angle forms a linear pair with 118°, so it is 180° - 118° = 62°.
So the four angles are 118°, 62°, 118°, 62°.
questions.explanation: One VO pair equal; the others are supplements.

questions.question: At a point O, three rays make angles (x)°, (2x)° and (3x)° all around O. Find each angle.
questions.answer:
Angles around a point sum to 360°: x + 2x + 3x = 360°.
6x = 360° => x = 60°.
The angles are 60°, 120° and 180°.

questions.question: List the four types of angle pairs formed when a transversal cuts two lines.
questions.answer: (1) Corresponding angles - same position at each crossing. (2) Alternate interior angles - between the lines, opposite sides of the transversal. (3) Alternate exterior angles - outside the lines, opposite sides. (4) Co-interior (allied/consecutive interior) angles - between the lines, same side of the transversal.
questions.explanation: Corresponding, alternate interior, alternate exterior, co-interior.

questions.question: For two parallel lines cut by a transversal, state which pairs are equal and which are supplementary.
questions.answer:
EQUAL: corresponding angles; alternate interior angles; alternate exterior angles.
SUPPLEMENTARY (sum 180°): co-interior (allied) angles.
questions.explanation: Corresponding and alternate equal; co-interior supplementary.

questions.question: How do co-interior angles differ from alternate interior angles?
questions.answer: Both lie BETWEEN the two lines (interior). The difference is the side of the transversal: ALTERNATE INTERIOR angles are on OPPOSITE sides of the transversal (and are equal for parallel lines), while CO-INTERIOR angles are on the SAME side (and are supplementary for parallel lines).
questions.explanation: Same side (co-interior, supplementary) vs opposite side (alternate, equal).

questions.question: AB || CD; a transversal makes a 75° angle. Find its corresponding, alternate and co-interior partners.
questions.answer: Corresponding angle = 75° (equal). Alternate interior angle = 75° (equal). Co-interior angle = 180° - 75° = 105° (supplementary).
questions.explanation: Equal for corresponding/alternate; 180 - x for co-interior.

questions.question: l || m; a transversal makes alternate interior angles (5x - 5)° and (3x + 25)°. Find x.
questions.answer:
Alternate interior angles are equal for parallel lines:
5x - 5 = 3x + 25 => 2x = 30 => x = 15.
Each angle = 5(15) - 5 = 70°.

questions.question: A transversal cuts two lines making corresponding angles 68° and 72°. Are the lines parallel? Why?
questions.answer: For the lines to be parallel, corresponding angles must be EQUAL. Here 68° is not equal to 72°, so the condition fails. Therefore the two lines are NOT parallel.

questions.question: l || m; co-interior angles are (2x + 20)° and (3x - 10)°. Find x and both angles.
questions.answer:
Co-interior angles are supplementary: (2x + 20) + (3x - 10) = 180.
5x + 10 = 180 => 5x = 170 => x = 34.
Angles: 2x + 20 = 88° and 3x - 10 = 92°. Check: 88 + 92 = 180.

questions.question: A ray on a line makes angles (4x - 10)° and (2x + 40)°. Find both angles.
In a figure, AB || CD. A transversal makes 3x with AB (interior) and the alternate interior angle at CD is (2x + 30)°. Find x and the angle.
questions.answer:
Alternate interior angles are equal: 3x = 2x + 30 => x = 30.
Each angle = 3x = 90° (also 2x + 30 = 90°).
questions.explanation: Alternate interior equal; solve for x.

questions.question: AB || CD and a transversal crosses both. If one angle at AB is 65°, find (a) the corresponding angle, (b) the co-interior angle, (c) the vertically opposite angle at the same crossing.
questions.answer:
(a) Corresponding angle at CD = 65° (corresponding angles equal).
(b) Co-interior angle at CD = 180° - 65° = 115° (allied, supplementary).
(c) Vertically opposite angle at the AB crossing = 65° (vertically opposite angles equal).
questions.explanation: Apply corresponding, co-interior and vertically-opposite rules.

questions.question: A transversal cuts two lines; the co-interior angles are (x + 30)° and (2x)°. For what x are the lines parallel?
questions.answer:
The lines are parallel exactly when the co-interior angles are supplementary:
(x + 30) + 2x = 180 => 3x + 30 = 180 => 3x = 150 => x = 50.
Then the angles are 80° and 100° (sum 180). So x = 50 makes the lines parallel.
questions.explanation: Set the co-interior sum to 180 and solve.

questions.question: Prove: if two lines are each perpendicular to the same line, they are parallel.
questions.answer: Let lines p and q both be perpendicular to line t. Where t meets p and where t meets q, each makes a 90° angle. Take t as a transversal cutting p and q: the two 90° angles at p and q that lie in corresponding positions are equal (both 90°). Since corresponding angles are equal, p || q. Hence two lines perpendicular to the same line are parallel.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Angles are classified by how much the arms open, measured in degrees. A full turn is 360°. Common classes are acute, right, obtuse, straight, reflex and complete.

(i) What is the range of an acute angle?
(ii) Classify 90° and 180°.
(iii) Classify 260°.
(iv) What is the reflex angle matching an ordinary angle of 100°?
questions.answer:
(i) An acute angle is greater than 0° and less than 90°.
(ii) 90° is a right angle; 180° is a straight angle.
(iii) 260° is a reflex angle (between 180° and 360°).
(iv) Reflex = 360° - 100° = 260°.
questions.explanation: Apply the standard measure ranges and the 360 rule.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Two angles are complementary if they add to 90° and supplementary if they add to 180°. The complement of x is (90 - x) and the supplement is (180 - x).

(i) Find the complement of 28°.
(ii) Find the supplement of 28°.
(iii) An angle equals its complement. Find it.
(iv) Can an angle of 130° have a complement? Why?
questions.answer:
(i) 90° - 28° = 62°.
(ii) 180° - 28° = 152°.
(iii) x = 90° - x => 2x = 90° => x = 45°.
(iv) No. Its complement would be 90° - 130° = -40°, which is impossible; only acute angles have complements.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Two supplementary angles are in the ratio 7 : 5.

(i) Write the two angles in terms of x.
(ii) Form an equation using the sum.
(iii) Solve for x.
(iv) State both angles.
questions.answer:
(i) The angles are 7x and 5x.
(ii) Supplementary => 7x + 5x = 180°.
(iii) 12x = 180° => x = 15°.
(iv) 7x = 105° and 5x = 75°. Check: 105 + 75 = 180.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Two straight lines AB and CD intersect at O. One of the four angles, angle AOC, is 72°.

(i) Find angle BOD.
(ii) Find angle AOD.
(iii) Find angle BOC.
(iv) State the two properties used.
questions.answer:
(i) angle BOD = 72° (vertically opposite to angle AOC).
(ii) angle AOD = 180° - 72° = 108° (linear pair with angle AOC).
(iii) angle BOC = 108° (vertically opposite to angle AOD).
(iv) Properties used: vertically opposite angles are equal; angles of a linear pair are supplementary.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

At a point O, four rays make angles around O of (2x)°, (3x)°, (4x)° and (3x)°.

(i) Write the equation for angles at a point.
(ii) Solve for x.
(iii) Find each angle.
(iv) Which is the largest?
questions.answer:
(i) Angles at a point sum to 360°: 2x + 3x + 4x + 3x = 360°.
(ii) 12x = 360° => x = 30°.
(iii) The angles are 60°, 90°, 120° and 90°.
(iv) The largest is 120° (the 4x angle).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A transversal cuts two parallel lines l and m, forming eight angles. The angle pairs have special names and relations.

(i) Name the pair that is equal and sits in the same position at each crossing.
(ii) Which interior pair is equal?
(iii) Which interior pair is supplementary?
(iv) State the relation for alternate exterior angles.
questions.answer:
(i) Corresponding angles - equal.
(ii) Alternate interior angles - equal.
(iii) Co-interior (allied) angles - supplementary (sum 180°).
(iv) Alternate exterior angles are equal (for parallel lines).
questions.explanation: Recall the four parallel-line angle relations.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

AB || CD and a transversal cuts them. An interior angle at AB measures 125°.

(i) Find the co-interior angle at CD.
(ii) Find the alternate interior angle at CD.
(iii) Find the corresponding angle at CD.
(iv) Give a reason for (i).
questions.answer:
(i) Co-interior angle = 180° - 125° = 55°.
(ii) Alternate interior angle = 125° (equal).
(iii) Corresponding angle = 125° (equal).
(iv) Reason: co-interior (allied) angles between parallel lines are supplementary, so they add to 180°.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

l || m and a transversal makes a pair of co-interior angles (4y)° and (5y)°.

(i) Form an equation.
(ii) Solve for y.
(iii) Find both angles.
(iv) What is the corresponding angle to the 4y angle?
questions.answer:
(i) Co-interior angles are supplementary: 4y + 5y = 180°.
(ii) 9y = 180° => y = 20°.
(iii) 4y = 80° and 5y = 100° (sum 180).
(iv) The corresponding angle to the 80° angle is also 80° (corresponding angles are equal).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The converse results let us test parallelism: equal corresponding (or alternate) angles, or supplementary co-interior angles, imply the lines are parallel.

(i) A transversal makes corresponding angles 85° and 85°. Parallel?
(ii) Alternate interior angles 60° and 65°. Parallel?
(iii) Co-interior angles 110° and 70°. Parallel?
(iv) Co-interior angles 100° and 90°. Parallel?
questions.answer:
(i) Yes - equal corresponding angles => parallel.
(ii) No - alternate interior angles are unequal (60 not = 65).
(iii) Yes - 110 + 70 = 180, co-interior supplementary => parallel.
(iv) No - 100 + 90 = 190, not 180, so not parallel.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

AB || CD. A transversal PQ crosses AB at E and CD at F. angle AEF (interior, at AB) = (3x)° and angle EFD (interior, at CD, same side) = (2x)°.

(i) What is the relation between these two angles?
(ii) Form and solve an equation.
(iii) Find both angles.
(iv) Find the alternate interior angle to angle AEF.
questions.answer:
(i) angle AEF and angle EFD are co-interior (allied) angles on the same side of the transversal, so they are supplementary.
(ii) 3x + 2x = 180° => 5x = 180° => x = 36°.
(iii) angle AEF = 3x = 108°; angle EFD = 2x = 72°.
(iv) The alternate interior angle to angle AEF (108°) is angle EFC = 108° (alternate interior angles are equal).
